claim: The TMEM175 family constitutes recently discovered K+ channels that are important for autophagosome turnover and lysosomal pH regulation.
source: The TMEM175 family constitutes recently discovered K+channels that are important for autophagosome turnover and lysosomal pH regulation and are associated with the early onset of Parkinson Disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research establishing TMEM175 function.

claim: TMEM175 channels are associated with the early onset of Parkinson Disease.
source: The TMEM175 family constitutes recently discovered K+channels that are important for autophagosome turnover and lysosomal pH regulation and are associated with the early onset of Parkinson Disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the introduction linking TMEM175 to Parkinson's disease through genome-wide association studies.

claim: TMEM175 channels lack a P-loop selectivity filter, a hallmark of all known K+ channels.
source: TMEM175 channels lack a P-loop selectivity filter, a hallmark of all known K+ channels, raising the question how selectivity is achieved.
evidence: This is established knowledge about canonical K+ channels and the structural difference of TMEM175.

claim: The X-ray structure of a closed bacterial TMEM175 channel in complex with a nanobody fusion-protein was solved at 2.4 Å resolution.
source: Here, we report the X-ray structure of a closed bacterial TMEM175 channel in complex with a nanobody fusion-protein disclosing bound K+ ions.
evidence: The resolution is stated in the methods and results sections with crystallographic data.

claim: A highly conserved layer of threonine residues in the pore conveys a basal K+ selectivity in TMEM175 channels.
source: Our analysis revealed that a highly conserved layer of threonine residues in the pore conveys a basal K+ selectivity.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and mutagenesis experiments showing loss of selectivity when threonines are mutated.

claim: An additional layer comprising two serines in human TMEM175 increases selectivity further.
source: An additional layer comprising two serines in human TMEM175 increases selectivity further and renders this channel sensitive to 4-aminopyridine and Zn2+.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data showing that S45A mutation reduces selectivity to bacterial levels.

claim: The additional serine layer in human TMEM175 renders this channel sensitive to 4-aminopyridine and Zn2+.
source: An additional layer comprising two serines in human TMEM175 increases selectivity further and renders this channel sensitive to 4-aminopyridine and Zn2+.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology experiments showing loss of blocker sensitivity in S45A mutant.

claim: Large hydrophobic side chains occlude the pore, forming a physical gate in TMEM175 channels.
source: Our findings suggest that large hydrophobic side chains occlude the pore, forming a physical gate, and that channel opening by iris-like motions simultaneously relocates the gate and exposes the otherwise concealed selectivity filter to the pore lumen.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis showing Leu35 occludes the pore in the closed state.

claim: Channel opening by iris-like motions simultaneously relocates the gate and exposes the otherwise concealed selectivity filter to the pore lumen.
source: Our findings suggest that large hydrophobic side chains occlude the pore, forming a physical gate, and that channel opening by iris-like motions simultaneously relocates the gate and exposes the otherwise concealed selectivity filter to the pore lumen.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural analysis and conservation patterns.

claim: Lysosomal membranes are permeable for K+ and even more so for Cs+.
source: It has been known for decades that lysosomal membranes are permeable for K+ and even more so for Cs+, a hallmark of this type of endo-membranes (Henning, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work from 1975.

claim: The TMEM175 channel was found to mediate a major K+ permeability of lysosomes and late endosomes.
source: The TMEM175 channel was found to mediate a major K+ permeability of lysosomes and late endosomes (hence also named KEL) (Cang et al., 2015), and is not related to canonical K+ channels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cang et al., 2015.

claim: TMEM175 channels are present in animals, eubacteria and archaea but are not found in plants and fungi.
source: TMEM175 channels are present in animals, eubacteria and archaea but are not found in plants and fungi.
evidence: This is based on sequence database searches and phylogenetic distribution.

claim: TMEM175 channels exhibit selectivities ranging from PK/PNa of ~35-20 in vertebrates to PK/PNa of ~2–5 in bacteria.
source: They exhibit selectivities ranging from PK/PNa of ~35-20 (Cang et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017) in vertebrates to PK/PNa of ~2–5 in bacteria and have been described as 'leak-like' channels (Cang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior electrophysiology studies.

claim: TMEM175 channels conduct Cs+ ions and are not blocked by Ba2+, tetraethylammonium or quinine.
source: TMEM175 channels, unlike canonical K+ channels, conduct Cs+ ions and are not blocked by Ba2+, tetraethylammonium or quinine but instead by Zn2+ ions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior pharmacological characterization.

claim: TMEM175 channels are blocked by Zn2+ ions.
source: TMEM175 channels, unlike canonical K+ channels, conduct Cs+ ions and are not blocked by Ba2+, tetraethylammonium or quinine but instead by Zn2+ ions.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in the manuscript and prior citations.

claim: TMEM175 channels are blocked by 4-aminopyridine (with the exception of bacterial TMEM175 proteins).
source: Like other K+ channels, they are blocked by 4-aminopyridine (with the exception of bacterial TMEM175 proteins), and conduct Rb+ but not Ca2+ and N-methyl-D-glucamine (Cang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data.

claim: TMEM175 channels conduct Rb+ but not Ca2+ and N-methyl-D-glucamine.
source: Like other K+ channels, they are blocked by 4-aminopyridine (with the exception of bacterial TMEM175 proteins), and conduct Rb+ but not Ca2+ and N-methyl-D-glucamine (Cang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Vertebrate TMEM175 proteins are composed of two homologous non-identical repeats, each comprising six transmembrane domains forming dimers.
source: The vertebrate TMEM175 proteins are composed of two homologous non-identical repeats, each comprising six transmembrane domains forming dimers; the bacterial homologues consist of only one such repeat and form tetramers (Cang et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Bacterial TMEM175 homologues consist of only one repeat and form tetramers.
source: The vertebrate TMEM175 proteins are composed of two homologous non-identical repeats, each comprising six transmembrane domains forming dimers; the bacterial homologues consist of only one such repeat and form tetramers (Cang et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations and SEC-MALLS data in the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of the TMEM175 gene leads to increased lysosomal pH under conditions of starvation.
source: In vertebrates, deletion of the TMEM175 gene leads to increased lysosomal pH under conditions of starvation, reduced proteolytic activity in lysosomes and aberrant autophagosome fusion and clearance (Cang et al., 2015; Jinn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: Deletion of the TMEM175 gene leads to reduced proteolytic activity in lysosomes.
source: In vertebrates, deletion of the TMEM175 gene leads to increased lysosomal pH under conditions of starvation, reduced proteolytic activity in lysosomes and aberrant autophagosome fusion and clearance (Cang et al., 2015; Jinn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: Deletion of the TMEM175 gene leads to aberrant autophagosome fusion and clearance.
source: In vertebrates, deletion of the TMEM175 gene leads to increased lysosomal pH under conditions of starvation, reduced proteolytic activity in lysosomes and aberrant autophagosome fusion and clearance (Cang et al., 2015; Jinn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: The human TMEM175 channel has been linked to Parkinson disease by several genome wide association studies.
source: The human TMEM175 channel has been linked to Parkinson disease (PD) by several genome wide association studies and is considered as a highly significant risk gene for the early onset of this neurodegenerative disease (Jinn et al., 2017; Nalls et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to GWAS studies.

claim: Human TMEM175 is considered as a highly significant risk gene for the early onset of Parkinson disease.
source: The human TMEM175 channel has been linked to Parkinson disease (PD) by several genome wide association studies and is considered as a highly significant risk gene for the early onset of this neurodegenerative disease (Jinn et al., 2017; Nalls et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to GWAS studies.

claim: The deficiency in autophagosome clearance and the impaired proteolytic activity by loss of TMEM175 are presumably causative for the accumulation of insoluble α-synuclein fibrils in PD models.
source: The deficiency in autophagosome clearance and the impaired proteolytic activity by loss of TMEM175 are presumably causative for the accumulation of insoluble α-synuclein fibrils in PD models and could explain why this channel is relevant for the progression of PD (Jinn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MtTMEM175 was crystallized in complex with a nanobody fused to an N-terminally truncated Maltose Binding Protein.
source: Finally, MtTMEM175 was crystallized in complex with a Nb that in turn was engineered by fusing an N-terminally truncated Maltose Binding Protein (MBP) to its C-terminus (Figure 1a,b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b) which greatly improved diffraction.
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown in figures.

claim: The structure was solved at a resolution of 2.4 Å using highly redundant data by molecular replacement.
source: We solved the structure at a resolution of 2.4 Å using highly redundant data by molecular replacement based on this novel Nb-MBP chaperone, with structures of Nbs and maltose-bound MBP as search models (Supplementary file 1) and could build a map of high quality (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and methods description.

claim: Each MtTMEM175 subunit is composed of six transmembrane helices.
source: Each MtTMEM175 subunit is composed of six transmembrane helices (Figure 1c) which assemble to form a tetrameric channel as verified using SEC-MALLS of uncomplexed MtTMEM175 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is shown in the structure and verified by SEC-MALLS.

claim: MtTMEM175 assembles to form a tetrameric channel.
source: Each MtTMEM175 subunit is composed of six transmembrane helices (Figure 1c) which assemble to form a tetrameric channel as verified using SEC-MALLS of uncomplexed MtTMEM175 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is verified by SEC-MALLS data.

claim: Helix one is the pore-lining helix in MtTMEM175.
source: Helix one is the pore-lining helix, as predicted earlier (Cang et al., 2015), and constitutes the highest degree of conservation (Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is shown in the structure and supported by prior predictions.

claim: Helix one constitutes the highest degree of conservation in TMEM175 channels.
source: Helix one is the pore-lining helix, as predicted earlier (Cang et al., 2015), and constitutes the highest degree of conservation (Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment and conservation analysis.

claim: MtTMEM175 exhibits non-rectifying, non-inactivating K+ currents that showed no signs of voltage-dependence.
source: In whole cell patch clamp experiments we recorded only from transfected cells non-rectifying, non-inactivating K+ currents that showed no signs of voltage-dependence (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data.

claim: MtTMEM175 currents were blocked by Zn2+ ions in a voltage-independent manner.
source: These currents were blocked by Zn2+ ions and at the applied concentration of 5 mM also in a voltage-independent manner (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data with Zn2+ application.

claim: MtTMEM175 has a low selectivity for K+ (PK/PNa ~ 4.3).
source: Similar to ScTMEM175 and CbTMEM175, MtTMEM175 has also a low selectivity for K+ (PK/PNa ~ 4.3).
evidence: This is calculated from reversal potential measurements.

claim: MtTMEM175 conducts Cs+ and Rb+ with a similar efficiency as K+.
source: It conducts Cs+ and Rb+ with a similar efficiency as K+, and to lesser extent, similar to Na+, also Li+ (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by ion substitution experiments in electrophysiology.

claim: MtTMEM175 conducts Li+ to a lesser extent, similar to Na+.
source: It conducts Cs+ and Rb+ with a similar efficiency as K+, and to lesser extent, similar to Na+, also Li+ (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by ion substitution experiments in electrophysiology.

claim: MtTMEM175 has no apparent permeability for anions.
source: The channel has no apparent permeability for anions; the reversal voltage was not significantly different when the same recordings were done with standard bath solution containing the large anion methanesulfonate (+0.64 ± 3 mV n = 18) or in a bath with 150 mM KCl (2.4 ± 4, n = 7).
evidence: This is shown by anion substitution experiments showing no change in reversal potential.

claim: Single channel recordings from MtTMEM175 revealed a unit conductance of ~70 pS.
source: We obtained a few single channel recordings from MtTMEM175-transfected cells that revealed a unit conductance of ~70 pS and showed channel flickering (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is measured from single channel recordings.

claim: Single channel recordings from MtTMEM175 showed channel flickering.
source: We obtained a few single channel recordings from MtTMEM175-transfected cells that revealed a unit conductance of ~70 pS and showed channel flickering (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is observed in single channel recordings.

claim: The presence of gating events in MtTMEM175 is inconsistent with the definition of a leak channel.
source: The presence of gating events is inconsistent with the definition of a leak channel and has significance for the interpretation of the structure.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of channel flickering.

claim: The MtTMEM175 structure revealed two densities attributable to K+ ions, termed 1K+ and 2K+.
source: The structure of MtTMEM175 revealed two densities attributable to K+ ions, termed 1K+ and 2K+ (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: This is shown in the electron density maps and anomalous scattering data.

claim: The presence of K+ at positions 1K+ and 2K+ is supported by data collection at higher wavelengths of 2.02460 Å.
source: The presence of K+ is supported by data collection at higher wavelengths of 2.02460 Å (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown by anomalous scattering data at wavelengths near the K absorption edge.

claim: One K+ ion (1K+) in the MtTMEM175 structure is located at an ion binding site at the extracellular pore entrance.
source: One K+ ion (1K+, occupancy ~1) in the MtTMEM175 structure, is located at an ion binding site at the extracellular pore entrance (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is shown in the structure with electron density.

claim: The K+ ion at 1K+ is complexed by eight water molecules in an anti-prismatic geometry.
source: The K+ ion is complexed by eight water molecules in an anti-prismatic geometry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) that are coordinated by backbone oxygens of Leu42, Ser43 and Ser44 (Figure 3b,d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is shown in the structure with detailed geometry analysis.

claim: The water molecules coordinating the K+ ion at 1K+ are coordinated by backbone oxygens of Leu42, Ser43 and Ser44.
source: The K+ ion is complexed by eight water molecules in an anti-prismatic geometry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) that are coordinated by backbone oxygens of Leu42, Ser43 and Ser44 (Figure 3b,d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is shown in the structure.

claim: The second K+ ion (2K+) is not coordinated by water molecules.
source: The second K+ ion (2K+, occupancy ~0.5) is not coordinated by water molecules which suggests the permeation of dehydrated K+ ions in these channels.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The lack of water coordination for the K+ ion at 2K+ suggests the permeation of dehydrated K+ ions in TMEM175 channels.
source: The second K+ ion (2K+, occupancy ~0.5) is not coordinated by water molecules which suggests the permeation of dehydrated K+ ions in these channels.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observation.

claim: The K+ ion at position 2K+ is located between the layers of Leu35 and Thr27.
source: The K+ ion at position 2K+ is located between the layers of Leu35 and Thr27 (Figure 3a,c).
evidence: This is shown in the structure.

claim: Soaking crystals with Cs+ and Rb+ revealed clear anomalous density for both ions at the position of 1K+.
source: By soaking crystals with Cs+ and Rb+ we detected clear anomalous density for both ions at the position of 1K+ (Figure 3e) providing additional evidence for an affinity towards monovalent cations with similar properties as K+ at this extracellular ion-binding site.
evidence: This is shown by anomalous scattering data from soaked crystals.

claim: No significant anomalous signal for Cs+ or Rb+ was found at the 2K+ position.
source: No significant anomalous signal for Cs+ or Rb+ was found at the 2K+ position, indicating that the channel would have to open for diffusion of these generally permeable ions to this position.
evidence: This is shown by anomalous scattering data.

claim: The absence of Cs+ or Rb+ at the 2K+ position indicates that the channel would have to open for diffusion of these ions to this position.
source: No significant anomalous signal for Cs+ or Rb+ was found at the 2K+ position, indicating that the channel would have to open for diffusion of these generally permeable ions to this position.
evidence: This is an inference from the anomalous scattering data.

claim: Leu35 is occluding the pore to such an extent that K+ ions could not pass in the MtTMEM175 structure.
source: In the structure of MtTMEM175 Leu35 is occluding the pore to such an extent that K+ ions could not pass (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown by pore radius calculations and structural analysis.

claim: Leu35 is likely constituting a hydrophobic physical gate in MtTMEM175.
source: This bulky residue is thus likely constituting a hydrophobic physical gate.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of pore occlusion.

claim: The structure of MtTMEM175 very likely represents a closed state.
source: Due to the highly constricted pore, the structure of MtTMEM175 thus very likely represents a closed state and this implies that structural rearrangements have to take place in order for the channel to become conductive.
evidence: This is inferred from pore radius analysis and single channel recordings showing gating.

claim: Structural rearrangements have to take place in order for MtTMEM175 to become conductive.
source: Due to the highly constricted pore, the structure of MtTMEM175 thus very likely represents a closed state and this implies that structural rearrangements have to take place in order for the channel to become conductive.
evidence: This is inferred from the closed state structure and functional data.

claim: Opening of the MtTMEM175 channel would inevitably require displacement of the hydrophobic side chain of Leu35 from the pore center.
source: Opening of the channel would inevitably require displacement of the hydrophobic side chain of Leu35 from the pore center, probably by a helix-rotation as seen in the NaK channel (Alam and Jiang, 2009a) or in TRPV6 (McGoldrick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the structure and comparison to other channels.

claim: Thr38 plays a pivotal role for K+ selectivity and conductance in MtTMEM175.
source: We thus conclude that Thr38 plays a pivotal role for K+ selectivity and conductance in MtTMEM175, reflected also in its high degree of conservation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data showing loss of selectivity in T38A mutant.

claim: The T38A mutant of MtTMEM175 showed a strongly impaired selectivity for K+ ions.
source: When analyzed in whole cell patch clamp recordings in HEK293 cells the T38A mutant of MtTMEM175 showed a strongly impaired selectivity for K+ ions, as exchanging K+ in the bath solution for Na+ caused only a minor shift of the reversal potential by –15 ± 2 mV (n = 4), corresponding to a PK/PNa < 2 (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data.

claim: The L35A mutant of MtTMEM175 showed only a slightly reduced selectivity compared to WT channels.
source: When we mutated Leu35 to alanine the channel showed only a slightly reduced selectivity compared to WT channels (Erev = −31 ± 2 mV, n = 6) (Figure 5b), in contrast to the findings on Ile23 for CmTMEM175 and Ile46/Ile271 in hTMEM175 (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data.

claim: The layer of threonines is conserved in vertebrate TMEM175 proteins.
source: The layer of threonines is also conserved in vertebrate TMEM175 proteins (Figure 5c) and we thus tested if mutating the corresponding residues to alanine in the human TMEM175 channel would affect selectivity.
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment.

claim: Human TMEM175 is more selective than the bacterial counterparts with reported values of PK/PNa of 35-20.
source: Human TMEM175 is more selective than the bacterial counterparts with reported values of PK/PNa of 35-20 (Cang et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The authors measured a PK/PNa value of ~10 for hTMEM175.
source: From the shift in the reversal voltage after replacing K+ for Na+ in the external medium (−58 ± 3, n = 7) we estimate a PK/PNa value of ~10 (Figure 5d), somewhat lower than the previously reported PK/PNa values of hTMEM175.
evidence: This is calculated from electrophysiology measurements.

claim: Mutating Thr49 in the first repeat and Thr274 in the second repeat of hTMEM175 to alanine resulted in strongly reduced selectivity.
source: Mutating Thr49 in the first repeat and Thr274 in the second repeat of hTMEM175 to alanine resulted in strongly reduced selectivity with a reversal potential of −17 ± 3 (n = 8) when exchanging K+ for Na+ in the external solution (Figure 5d), providing evidence for a conserved role of the threonine-layer in selectivity.
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data on the mutant.

claim: The position corresponding to Ala34 in MtTMEM175 is occupied by serine in repeat one for all analyzed vertebrate species.
source: When comparing the primary sequences of vertebrate genes, we found that the position that is corresponding to the highly conserved Ala34 in MtTMEM175 is occupied by serine in repeat one for all of the analyzed vertebrate species (Ser45 in hTMEM175), while in repeat 2, like in bacterial channels, the corresponding residue is an alanine (Ala270 in hTMEM175) (Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1e,f).
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment.

claim: In repeat 2 of vertebrate TMEM175, the position corresponding to Ala34 in MtTMEM175 is an alanine (Ala270 in hTMEM175).
source: When comparing the primary sequences of vertebrate genes, we found that the position that is corresponding to the highly conserved Ala34 in MtTMEM175 is occupied by serine in repeat one for all of the analyzed vertebrate species (Ser45 in hTMEM175), while in repeat 2, like in bacterial channels, the corresponding residue is an alanine (Ala270 in hTMEM175) (Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1e,f).
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment.

claim: In the S45A mutant of hTMEM175, selectivity was reduced with a reversal potential of −27 ± 2 (n = 24) upon changing the major cation in the bath solution from K+ to Na+.
source: In the S45A mutant dimer, selectivity was indeed reduced with a reversal potential of −27 ± 2 (n = 24) upon changing the major cation in the bath solution from K+ to Na+.
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data.

claim: The S45A mutant of hTMEM175 is very similar to bacterial TMEM175 channels in its primary sequence of helix one and with respect to its preference for K+.
source: This mutant is very similar to bacterial TMEM175 channels in its primary sequence of helix one and intriguingly also with respect to its preference for K+.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence comparison and electrophysiology data.

claim: A triple mutant (S45A/T49A/T274A) of hTMEM175 shows a similar reduction of selectivity as the double mutant T49A/T249A and the T38A mutant protein of MtTMEM175.
source: Consequently, a triple mutant where all of the threonine and serine residues in these two layers of the pore are exchanged for alanine (S45A/T49A/T274A) shows a similar reduction of selectivity (Erev = −22 ± 3 mV, n = 8) (Figure 5d) as the double mutant T49A/T249A and the T38A mutant protein of MtTMEM175 (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data.

claim: Ser45 in the first repeat is accounting for the increased selectivity of the human TMEM175 channel, but in conjunction with the threonine layer.
source: We thus conclude that Ser45 in the first repeat is accounting for the increased selectivity of the human TMEM175 channel, but in conjunction with the threonine layer.
evidence: This is concluded from mutagenesis data showing effects of both serine and threonine mutations.

claim: Human TMEM175 is substantially more sensitive to Zn2+ ions than bacterial TMEM175 channels (IC50 ~38 µM compared to an estimated IC50 of ~0.5 mM).
source: In comparison to bacterial TMEM175 channels, the human TMEM175 channel is substantially more sensitive to Zn2+ ions (IC50 ~38 µM compared to an estimated IC50 of ~0.5 mM for bacterial homologues [Cang et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The human TMEM175 channel is inhibited by the potassium-channel blocker 4-AP (IC50 ~35 µM).
source: In addition, the human channel is also inhibited by the potassium-channel blocker 4-AP (IC50 ~35 µM) (Cang et al., 2015), indicating significant differences between human and bacterial homologues and suggesting a more specific interaction of the blockers with the human channel.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The equally effective block of human TMEM175 by Zn2+ and 4-AP regardless of extracellular or intracellular application is a good indication that the block is occurring in the pore.
source: The equally effective block of human TMEM175 by Zn2+ and 4-AP regardless of extracellular or intracellular application (Cang et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017) is a good indication that the block is occurring in the pore.
evidence: This is inferred from prior functional data cited.

claim: The S45A mutant of hTMEM175 is not blocked by Zn2+ ions.
source: As shown in Figure 6a and b, the S45A mutant is not blocked by Zn2+ ions and also lost its sensitivity for 4-AP at a concentration of 100 µM.
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data.

claim: The S45A mutant of hTMEM175 lost its sensitivity for 4-AP at a concentration of 100 µM.
source: As shown in Figure 6a and b, the S45A mutant is not blocked by Zn2+ ions and also lost its sensitivity for 4-AP at a concentration of 100 µM.
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data.

claim: Both Zn2+ and 4-AP act as pore blockers at the selectivity filter in hTMEM175.
source: These data confirm that both Zn2+ and 4-AP act as pore blockers at the selectivity filter, at very similar locations.
evidence: This is concluded from the S45A mutant data.

claim: The T38A mutant of MtTMEM175 retained its sensitivity for Zn2+.
source: Indeed, the T38A mutant of MtTMEM175 retained its sensitivity for Zn2+; in WT and the mutant channel Zn2+ caused at a reference voltage of −60 mV the same relative inhibition (WT 66.9 ± 12%, T38A mutant 69.7 ± 10 n = 4) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data.

claim: Anomalous signal of Zn2+ ions was clearly localized in the pore by soaking crystals of MtTMEM175 with 0.5 mM Zn2+.
source: In seeming contrast to this finding we could clearly localize anomalous signal of Zn2+ ions in the pore by soaking crystals of MtTMEM175 with 0.5 mM Zn2+.
evidence: This is shown by anomalous scattering data.

claim: The major peak of Zn2+ anomalous signal lies in proximity to Thr38 and Leu35 in MtTMEM175.
source: The major peak of this anomalous signal (when contoured at 4σ) lies in proximity to Thr38 and Leu35 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is shown by anomalous scattering data.

claim: In crystal soaking experiments with the T38A mutant of MtTMEM175, no anomalous signal for Zn was detected even when using concentrations of 2.5 mM.
source: In crystal soaking experiments with the T38A mutant of MtTMEM175 we could not detect anomalous signal for Zn, even when using concentrations of 2.5 mM (0.5–2.5 mM tested) and contouring of the anomalous signal at 4σ and 2σ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is shown by anomalous scattering data.

claim: The T38A mutation changes the electrostatic environment in the pore of MtTMEM175.
source: This supports an attraction for Zn2+ ions in the pore in close distance to, or directly at the selectivity filter and indicates that the T38A mutation changes the electrostatic environment in the pore.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of Zn2+ binding in the T38A mutant structure.

claim: The functional analysis does not support the idea that Zn2+ is blocking MtTMEM175 by the same mechanism as hTMEM175.
source: However, our functional analysis does not support the idea that Zn2+ is blocking MtTMEM175 by the same mechanism as hTMEM175.
evidence: This is concluded from the different effects of mutations on Zn2+ sensitivity.

claim: Aberrant processing of autophagosomes as well as an increased lysosomal pH under conditions of starvation is the prominent phenotype of TMEM175-loss.
source: Even though its exact function in lysosomal physiology still needs to be clarified the available experimental evidence shows that aberrant processing of autophagosomes as well as an increased lysosomal pH under conditions of starvation is the prominent phenotype of TMEM175-loss (Cang et al., 2015; Jinn et al., 2017) and likely connects this lysosomal pathology to PD.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The TMEM175 ion pathway is built from an ion binding site for monovalent cations at the extracellular pore entrance.
source: From the structural analysis we divide the pore of TMEM175 channels into functional layers (Figure 7a), conceptually different from a previous interpretation (Lee et al., 2017): The TMEM175 ion pathway is built from an ion binding site for monovalent cations (with properties similar to K+ ions) at the extracellular pore entrance, a major gate at the position of Leu35 (MtTMEM175) and, rather unusual, by one (in prokaryotes) or two interspersed polar layers (in vertebrates) that tune K+ selectivity.
evidence: This is concluded from structural and functional analysis.

claim: The TMEM175 ion pathway has a major gate at the position of Leu35 in MtTMEM175.
source: From the structural analysis we divide the pore of TMEM175 channels into functional layers (Figure 7a), conceptually different from a previous interpretation (Lee et al., 2017): The TMEM175 ion pathway is built from an ion binding site for monovalent cations (with properties similar to K+ ions) at the extracellular pore entrance, a major gate at the position of Leu35 (MtTMEM175) and, rather unusual, by one (in prokaryotes) or two interspersed polar layers (in vertebrates) that tune K+ selectivity.
evidence: This is concluded from structural and functional analysis.

claim: The TMEM175 ion pathway has one (in prokaryotes) or two interspersed polar layers (in vertebrates) that tune K+ selectivity.
source: From the structural analysis we divide the pore of TMEM175 channels into functional layers (Figure 7a), conceptually different from a previous interpretation (Lee et al., 2017): The TMEM175 ion pathway is built from an ion binding site for monovalent cations (with properties similar to K+ ions) at the extracellular pore entrance, a major gate at the position of Leu35 (MtTMEM175) and, rather unusual, by one (in prokaryotes) or two interspersed polar layers (in vertebrates) that tune K+ selectivity.
evidence: This is concluded from structural and functional analysis.

claim: A rotation of helix 1 results in an iris-like opening in assembled TMEM175 channels as a plausible route for transitioning into a conductive conformation.
source: But since these residues do not face the pore lumen we anticipate a rotation of helix 1, resulting in an iris-like opening in assembled TMEM175 channels as a plausible route for transitioning into a conductive conformation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural analysis.

claim: In hTMEM175, the selectivity could be attenuated to levels of bacterial homologues by reducing the number of coordinating ligands from six to four through mutation of Ser45 to alanine.
source: Intriguingly, in hTMEM175 the selectivity could be attenuated to levels of bacterial homologues by reducing the number of coordinating ligands from six to four through mutation of Ser45 to alanine.
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data on the S45A mutant.

claim: Ser45 is underlying a pore block by Zn2+ and 4-AP in hTMEM175 at the site of the selectivity filter.
source: The proposed mechanism for K+ selectivity in TMEM175 channels is also backed by our finding that Ser45 is underlying a pore block by Zn2+ and 4-AP in hTMEM175 at the site of the selectivity filter, underscoring that the respective Ser residues are part of the conductive pathway.
evidence: This is concluded from the loss of blocker sensitivity in the S45A mutant.

claim: The voltage independence of the pore block in hTMEM175 is unusual for a binding site in the electric field of the channel.
source: Another unusual finding is the voltage independence of the pore block in hTMEM175 (Figure 6a), as this is expected for a binding site in the electric field of the channel (Hilf et al., 2010).
evidence: This is observed in electrophysiology data and compared to expectations from prior work.

claim: TMEM175 channels spontaneously open and close without a trigger, different from voltage- or ligand-gated ion channels.
source: We can currently only speculate but one reason could be that TMEM175 channels spontaneously open and close without a trigger, different from voltage- or ligand-gated ion channels.
evidence: This is speculated based on the voltage-independent block and single channel recordings.

claim: MtTMEM175 was crystallized at a pH of 8.5.
source: Since MtTMEM175 was crystallized at a pH of 8.5 and CmTMEM175 at a pH of 4.5 it is most likely that His73 in CmTMEM175 (corresponding to His77 in MtTMEM175) is protonated and hence repulsing the arginine.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: CmTMEM175 was crystallized at a pH of 4.5.
source: Since MtTMEM175 was crystallized at a pH of 8.5 and CmTMEM175 at a pH of 4.5 it is most likely that His73 in CmTMEM175 (corresponding to His77 in MtTMEM175) is protonated and hence repulsing the arginine.
evidence: This is inferred from the prior publication on CmTMEM175.

claim: A transient pH-sensitive disengagement of the arginine from the histidine could be a step in the opening of TMEM175 channels.
source: A transient pH-sensitive disengagement of this arginine from the histidine (and Asp30) could be a step in the opening of the channel.
evidence: This is speculated based on structural differences between MtTMEM175 and CmTMEM175.

claim: The CmTMEM175 structure shows a more open pore at the intracellular side compared to MtTMEM175.
source: This would be achieved by loosening interactions of the N-terminal end of helix one with the adjacent subunit as already indicated in the CmTMEM175 structure which shows a more open pore at the intracellular side compared to MtTMEM175 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is shown by pore radius calculations comparing the two structures.

claim: Only the extracellular end of helix one in the CmTMEM175 structure contains a 310-helix over a stretch of 3–4 residues.
source: Notably, only the extracellular end of helix one in the CmTMEM175 structure contains a 310-helix over a stretch of 3–4 residues and thus extends further than helix one in MtTMEM175 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f,g).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the two structures.

claim: The backbone oxygens in CmTMEM175 are too distant from the pore axis for interacting with the water molecules of a K+-hydrate.
source: As a consequence the backbone oxygens are too distant from the pore axis for interacting, like in the MtTMEM175 structure, with the water molecules of a K+-hydrate (Figure 3a,b,d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1i,k).
evidence: This is concluded from structural comparison.

claim: The short helix between the helices 1 and 2 of CmTMEM175 is involved in major crystal contacts.
source: It is furthermore worth noting, that the short helix between the helices 1 and 2 of CmTMEM175 is involved in major crystal contacts, which might be responsible for a displacement of the tips of helix1 and formation of the 310-helix (Figure 3—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is observed in the CmTMEM175 structure.

claim: Mutation of Ile23 or corresponding residues in hTMEM175 to small or hydrophilic residues resulted in a loss of K+ selectivity according to Lee et al., 2017.
source: Mutation of Ile23 or corresponding residues in hTMEM175 to small or hydrophilic residues indeed resulted in a loss of K+ selectivity (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: If Ile23 acts as a gate to keep the channel closed, an exchange for asparagine or alanine would likely result in a permanently open channel.
source: If Ile23 however acts as a gate to keep the channel closed, a role that we suggest for the corresponding Leu35 in MtTMEM175, an exchange for asparagine or alanine would likely result in a permanently open channel (Figure 6—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison to other channels where gate mutations cause opening.

claim: In bestrophins, mutation of three layers of bulky residues along the ion path to alanine resulted in an open channel, without the requirement for activation.
source: For instance, in bestrophins, mutation of three layers of bulky residues along the ion path to alanine resulted in an open channel, without the requirement for activation (Vaisey et al., 2016; Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from prior work on bestrophins.

claim: A cryo-EM structure of chicken bestrophin in a conductive conformation provided evidence against a role of the bulky pore-occluding residues as hydrophobic selectivity filters.
source: More recently a cryo-EM structure of chicken bestrophin in a conductive conformation provided evidence against a role of the bulky pore-occluding residues as hydrophobic selectivity filters but instead revealed that these residues are indeed physical gates (Miller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from recent work on bestrophins.

claim: TMEM175 channels recapitulate classical structure-function correlates of other ion channel families: Large hydrophobic residues are acting as gates and polar contacts from side chains and the backbone are coordinating ions in the conducting pathway.
source: TMEM175 channels are not as enigmatic as anticipated earlier but instead recapitulate classical structure-function correlates of other ion channel families: Large hydrophobic residues are acting as gates and polar contacts from side chains and the backbone are coordinating ions in the conducting pathway.
evidence: This is concluded from the structural and functional analysis.

claim: The selectivity in TMEM175 is mediated by cryptic hydroxyl-bearing side chains inside the pore that are only available for selective ion solvation in an open conformation by concerted repositioning.
source: On the other hand, it is remarkable that the selectivity is mediated by cryptic hydroxyl-bearing side chains inside the pore that are only available for selective ion solvation in an open conformation by concerted repositioning.
evidence: This is concluded from the structural and functional analysis.

claim: The conductive state of TMEM175 must deviate substantially from the closed state in order to be permeable to ions.
source: In conclusion, the conductive state must thus deviate substantially from the closed state in order to be permeable to ions.
evidence: This is concluded from the structural and functional analysis.

claim: The localization of the residues that mediate K+ selectivity and sensitivity to the blockers Zn2+ and 4-AP strongly supports that the conductive state deviates substantially from the closed state.
source: This is strongly supported by the localization of the residues that mediate K+ selectivity and sensitivity to the blockers Zn2+ and 4-AP.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutagenesis and structural data.
